en: When one whose intellect has been purified by austerity, sacrifice, charity, and other means becomes dispassionate toward the status of kings and the like through the realization of their worthlessness, and having renounced everything, attains that supreme reality which is the eternal Brahman—that alone am I. || 1 ||

Having propitiated a compassionate Guru who is established in Brahman and profoundly tranquil, and having reflected upon one's own true nature through the intellect, the wise man attains the reality through constant meditation; that Supreme Brahman is eternally "I am That. || 2 ||

That which is of the nature of bliss, whose essence is light, from which the phenomenal world has vanished, which is devoid of all limitations, accessible solely through the mental state of "I am Brahman," and is the supreme Fourth (Turīya)—that eternal Supreme Brahman alone am I. 3.
That from whose ignorance the entire universe appears, and which vanishes instantly upon the awakening of the Self;
that which transcends mind and speech, pure, liberated, the Supreme Brahman, eternal—that alone am I. 4.

When negation has been performed through such statements as "not this, not this," that which appears to those established in samādhi—complete, transcending the three states, non-dual, one, the supreme Brahman, eternal—that alone am I. 5.
When the universe was made to rejoice by mere fragments of that bliss, and when everything shines within the essence, then all else appears as its light;
that eternal Supreme Brahman alone am I.

I am that very eternal Supreme Brahman—endless, all-pervading, free from conceptual construction, effortless, auspicious, devoid of attachment, accessible through the syllable Om, formless, intensely radiant, and beyond death. 7.
O Ānanda, when a person is submerged in the ocean, the entire phenomenal world, which is the play of ignorance, ceases to appear;
that for which this occurs is the eternal Supreme Brahman, and I am indeed that very one—this is our wondrous realization. 8.

The man who, with a spirit of devotion, recites this hymn consisting of the contemplation of the essential nature [of the Lord] with reverence, or hears it here constantly with a mind ever-alert, shall become Viṣṇu even in this very life, according to the authority of the Vedas. (9)

Thus ends "The Octave on the Contemplation of One's True Nature," composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).
